newsitem.title: USA: Lawmaker sees no power market threat to clean air.
newsitem.headline: Lawmaker sees no power market threat to clean air.

text.p: A key U.S. lawmaker Tuesday dismissed concerns that power market competition would spark a wave of new pollution from coal-fired power plants.

Northeastern states and green groups are concerned that in an open power market, Midwestern coal-fired plants will become a cheap source of power and will boost their output, blowing pollution into the Northeast.

But Rep. Dan Schaefer, chairman of the House Energy and Power subcommittee, said railroad capacity would limit the amount of coal available for those power plants, restricting their ability to increase power production.
"You can only put so many coal trains on a track," the Colorado Republican said at a luncheon for energy lobbyists.
"It's going to be difficult for coal plants to beef up another 15 or 20 pecent simply because of the transportation situation," he said.
Schaefer and Commerce Committee chairman Tom Bliley are leading the effort to break up utility monopolies.
Schaefer said repeated his view that there was no need to open the Clean Air Act to accommodate changes in the power market.

"We think it's covered in the Clean Air Act," he said, adding that states that could not meet air quality standards could already petition the Environmental Protection Agency to order new pollution controls if necessary.
